Bayesian calibration with brms

Source: vignettes/bayesian-calibration.Rmd
bayesian-calibration.Rmd

The calibration of vignette("calibration") fits the candidate models by maximum likelihood with ‘lme4’. sheepdog can also fit the selected model in a Bayesian framework with ‘brms’. This gives three things the maximum likelihood fit does not:

  • the uncertainty of the calibrated probability of every detection, and a rule that uses it (“is P(TP) >= p_min with high posterior probability?”) instead of a point estimate;
  • priors that regularise the variance components, which avoids the singular fits that ‘lme4’ gives when a correlation or a variance is estimated at the boundary;
  • the propagation of the calibration uncertainty to the detection histories and the community matrices.

The cost is computing time and the need to state, and check, a prior. The workflow below follows the steps of a Bayesian workflow: prior predictive check, fit, convergence diagnostics, posterior predictive check and sensitivity to the prior (Gelman et al. 2026; McElreath 2020).

library(sheepdog)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
ex <- system.file("extdata", "example", package = "sheepdog")
val_files <- list.files(file.path(ex, "validation"), full.names = TRUE)
val <- suppressMessages(read_validations(val_files))

The model

We use the model retained by the log-loss rule in vignette("calibration"): species slopes and intercepts without their correlation, and site x species intercepts.

f <- calibration_models(uncorrelated = TRUE)$m5_species_x_site_uncorrelated
f
#> tp ~ logit_conf + (1 | species) + (0 + logit_conf | species) + 
#>     (1 | site:species)
#> <environment: 0x7725e09658>

The prior

fit_calibration(engine = "brms") requires the prior to be given explicitly: ‘brms’ would otherwise use flat priors on the slopes. calibration_prior() builds a weakly informative example centred on the hypothesis that the BirdNET score is already calibrated, P(TP) = score. The data then show how far the classifier departs from it.

prior <- calibration_prior(f, val)
prior
#>               prior     class coef group resp dpar nlpar   lb   ub tag source
#>  normal(0.913, 1.5) Intercept                            <NA> <NA>       user
#>        normal(1, 1)         b                               0 <NA>       user
#>      exponential(1)        sd                            <NA> <NA>       user
  • The slope of logit_conf is centred on 1 (a calibrated score), with a standard deviation of 1, and truncated at 0: a higher score never lowers P(TP).
  • ‘brms’ centres the predictors, so the intercept is the logit of P(TP) at the mean logit score of the reviewed clips (0.913); centring its prior on that value makes slope 1 and intercept equal to the mean correspond to P(TP) = score.
  • The standard deviations of the species and site x species effects get exponential(1), most of whose mass lies on moderate differences on the logit scale.

Prior predictive check

Before fitting, sample the model from the prior alone and look at the calibration curves it implies on the probability scale. plot_calibration_draws() draws the population-level curve of 100 draws:

prior_fit <- prior_predictive_calibration(
  f, val, prior, chains = 2, iter = 1000, refresh = 0, silent = 2,
  backend = "cmdstanr", seed = 2026)
#> Carregando namespace exigido: rstan
plot_calibration_draws(prior_fit)
plot of chunk prior-check

The prior allows curves well above and well below the diagonal (a calibrated score), all increasing; it rules out nothing a reviewer would consider plausible, and it does not force the curves to cross p_min at any particular score.

Fitting 

fit <- fit_calibration(val, f, engine = "brms", prior = prior,
                       chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000,
                       control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
                       refresh = 0, silent = 2, backend = "cmdstanr",
                       seed = 2026)

fit_calibration() runs calibration_diagnostics() after the fit and warns when the largest R-hat exceeds 1.01, the bulk or tail effective sample sizes fall below 400, or there are divergent transitions:

calibration_diagnostics(fit)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   max_rhat min_ess_bulk min_ess_tail n_divergent ok   
#>      <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>       <int> <lgl>
#> 1     1.01         788.        1450.           0 TRUE

A higher adapt_delta (here 0.95) is the first remedy for divergent transitions; persistent divergences point to a model that the data cannot identify.

summary(fit)$fixed
#>             Estimate Est.Error   l-95% CI  u-95% CI     Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> Intercept  -0.391735 0.3658406 -1.1143408 0.3468419 1.000501 2388.154 2612.636
#> logit_conf  2.093138 0.5675039  0.9230704 3.1608814 1.003420 1280.111 1747.844

Posterior predictive check

The observed proportion of true positives by species should fall within the distribution of the proportions replicated from the posterior:

brms::pp_check(fit, type = "stat_grouped", group = "species",
               stat = "mean", ndraws = 500)
plot of chunk ppc

Sensitivity to the prior

calibration_sensitivity() runs the power-scaling analysis of ‘priorsense’ (Kallioinen et al. 2024): it measures how much each population-level parameter and each standard deviation changes when the prior or the likelihood is up- or down-weighted.

sens <- calibration_sensitivity(fit)
sens
#> Sensitivity based on cjs_dist
#> Prior selection: all priors
#> Likelihood selection: all data
#> 
#>                    variable prior likelihood
#>                 b_Intercept 0.030      0.024
#>                b_logit_conf 0.119      0.039
#>  sd_site:species__Intercept 0.055      0.157
#>       sd_species__Intercept 0.112      0.076
#>      sd_species__logit_conf 0.126      0.048
#>                                 diagnosis
#>                                         -
#>  potential strong prior / weak likelihood
#>       potential prior-likelihood conflict
#>       potential prior-likelihood conflict
#>  potential strong prior / weak likelihood

A parameter sensitive to the prior but not to the likelihood (“strong prior / weak likelihood”) is mostly determined by the prior; one sensitive to both (“prior-likelihood conflict”) is pulled in different directions by the prior and the data. Here the flagged standard deviations are sd_site:species__Intercept, sd_species__Intercept, sd_species__logit_conf, and the flagged population-level parameters are b_logit_conf. The standard deviations of the species effects, and the population slope (the mean of the species slopes), are estimated from only 8 species, so their prior matters. Two things follow. Report the prior together with the results. And check that the conclusions (the calibrated probabilities near p_min, the detection histories) do not change under a wider prior, for instance normal(1, 2) on the slope: with ‘priorsense’ this is what the power-scaling approximates without refitting. With more species, the likelihood takes over and the flags disappear.

Posterior calibration curves 

plot_calibration_draws(fit)
plot of chunk posterior-curves

The population-level curves are steeper than the diagonal (posterior mean slope 2.09, 95 % interval 0.92 to 3.16): in the example, low scores overestimate P(TP) and high scores underestimate it. The curves by species and site, with the observed precision by score bin, are drawn by plot_calibration() as for the ‘lme4’ fit:

plot_calibration(fit, val)
plot of chunk curves

Scoring the detections

score_detections() computes the posterior of P(TP) once on a grid of scores (step 0.01) for each site x species, and assigns it to the detections by their rounded score; the cost does not depend on the number of detections. Each detection gets the posterior mean (p_tp), a lower quantile (p_tp_lower, 5 % by default) and the posterior probability that P(TP) >= p_min (pr_reliable):

sites <- c("ARA", "BAI", "NHE", "XAR")
tables <- setNames(file.path(ex, "birdnet", sites,
                             "BirdNET_SelectionTable.txt"), sites)
scored <- suppressMessages(score_detections(tables, fit, p_min = 0.95))
scored |>
  select(site, species, confidence, p_tp, p_tp_lower, pr_reliable) |>
  arrange(desc(confidence)) |>
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   site  species confidence  p_tp p_tp_lower pr_reliable
#>   <chr> <chr>        <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 NHE   phy_cuv      0.995 1.000      1.000           1
#> 2 NHE   lep_pod      0.993 1.000      1.000           1
#> 3 XAR   lep_pod      0.993 1.000      1.000           1
#> 4 NHE   ela_bic      0.992 1.000      1.000           1
#> 5 ARA   boa_ran      0.991 1.000      1.000           1
#> 6 ARA   lep_pod      0.991 1.000      1.000           1

Two rules for a reliable detection

detection_history() can count a detection as reliable when its posterior mean reaches p_min (rule = "mean", as with ‘lme4’) or when the posterior probability that P(TP) >= p_min reaches prob_min (rule = "probability"):

h_mean <- detection_history(scored, p_min = 0.95)
h_prob <- detection_history(scored, p_min = 0.95, rule = "probability",
                            prob_min = 0.9)
tibble(rule = c("mean", "probability"),
       nights_k1 = c(sum(h_mean$detection_k1), sum(h_prob$detection_k1)),
       nights_k2 = c(sum(h_mean$detection_k2), sum(h_prob$detection_k2)))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   rule        nights_k1 nights_k2
#>   <chr>           <int>     <int>
#> 1 mean              357       322
#> 2 probability       339       306

The probability rule is more conservative where the calibration is uncertain, typically in cells with few reviewed clips, because it asks that the calibrated probability exceed p_min with high posterior probability rather than on average.

inner_join(count(h_mean, species, wt = detection_k1, name = "mean"),
           count(h_prob, species, wt = detection_k1, name = "probability"),
           by = "species")
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   species  mean probability
#>   <chr>   <int>       <int>
#> 1 boa_ran    68          68
#> 2 den_nan    30          21
#> 3 ela_bic    85          85
#> 4 lep_fus     3           0
#> 5 lep_pod    78          78
#> 6 phy_cuv    81          81
#> 7 pse_pla     0           0
#> 8 sci_nas    12           6

Propagating the uncertainty to the community matrices

Both rules still produce a single history. history_draws() rebuilds the history for each of n_draws posterior draws: in a draw, a detection is reliable when its probability in that draw is >= p_min. The cost is again independent of the number of detections.

hd <- history_draws(fit, scored, p_min = 0.95, n_draws = 200)
hd
#> # A tibble: 174,400 × 10
#>     draw site  species night   n_detections n_reliable detection_k1 detection_k2
#>    <int> <chr> <chr>   <chr>          <int>      <int>        <int>        <int>
#>  1    33 ARA   boa_ran 202110…           10          2            1            1
#>  2    33 ARA   boa_ran 202110…           13          9            1            1
#>  3    33 ARA   boa_ran 202110…           16         10            1            1
#>  4    33 ARA   boa_ran 202110…           11          5            1            1
#>  5    33 ARA   boa_ran 202110…            8          3            1            1
#>  6    33 ARA   boa_ran 202111…           13          9            1            1
#>  7    33 ARA   boa_ran 202111…            9          5            1            1
#>  8    33 ARA   boa_ran 202111…           11          4            1            1
#>  9    33 ARA   boa_ran 202111…           12          7            1            1
#> 10    33 ARA   boa_ran 202111…            7          3            1            1
#> # ℹ 174,390 more rows
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: detection_k3 <int>, detection <int>

community_matrices_draws() builds the community matrices of community_matrices() for each draw and summarises each site x month x species frequency by its posterior mean and a 90 % interval:

core <- c("boa_ran", "ela_bic", "lep_pod", "phy_cuv")
md <- community_matrices_draws(hd, core, k_min = 2, min_nights_month = 5)
md$summary |>
  mutate(width = frequency_upper - frequency_lower) |>
  arrange(desc(width)) |>
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   site  month   species n_nights_recorded frequency_mean frequency_lower
#>   <chr> <chr>   <chr>               <int>          <dbl>           <dbl>
#> 1 ARA   2022-01 lep_pod                 5          0.79              0.6
#> 2 XAR   2021-11 boa_ran                 5          0.918             0.6
#> 3 NHE   2021-11 boa_ran                 5          0.777             0.6
#> 4 XAR   2021-12 lep_pod                 5          0.62              0.6
#> 5 ARA   2021-12 ela_bic                 5          0.986             0.8
#> 6 BAI   2021-12 boa_ran                 5          0.834             0.8
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: frequency_upper <dbl>, width <dbl>

12 of the 92 site x month x species cells have a frequency that changes among draws; the others are fixed because their detections are far above or below p_min in every draw.

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(md$summary, aes(month, frequency_mean, colour = site, group = site)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = frequency_lower, ymax = frequency_upper),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), size = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ species) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Frequency of nights with detection (k = 2)",
       subtitle = "Posterior mean and 90 % interval over 200 draws") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
plot of chunk matrix-uncertainty

md$draws keeps the frequency of every draw, so that a downstream analysis (an ordination, a GLLVM; see vignette("community-matrices")) can be repeated on each draw and its results summarised over draws.

The calibrate() wrapper

calibrate() takes the same options. The comparison of the candidate models still uses maximum likelihood, which is fast; the selected model is then refitted with ‘brms’. Passing prior = calibration_prior (the function) builds the example prior for whichever model is selected:

res <- calibrate(val_files, tables, output_dir = "calibration",
                 select = "one_se_logloss", uncorrelated = TRUE,
                 engine = "brms", prior = calibration_prior,
                 brms_args = list(chains = 4, cores = 4,
                                  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
                                  backend = "cmdstanr"),
                 rule = "probability", prob_min = 0.9)

calibrate() then also writes calibration_diagnostics.csv.

References

Gelman, A., Vehtari, A., McElreath, R., Simpson, D., Margossian, C. C., Yao, Y., Kennedy, L., Gabry, J., Bürkner, P.-C., Modrák, M., & Leos Barajas, V. (2026). Bayesian Workflow. Chapman & Hall. https://avehtari.github.io/Bayesian-Workflow/

Kallioinen, N., Paananen, T., Bürkner, P.-C., & Vehtari, A. (2024). Detecting and diagnosing prior and likelihood sensitivity with power-scaling. Statistics and Computing, 34, 57. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-023-10366-5

McElreath, R. (2020). Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R and Stan (2nd ed.). Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/9780429029608
